mcqs.question: Which of the following best defines a random experiment in probability?

options.A: An experiment whose outcome is predetermined and known in advance.
options.B: An experiment that can be performed only once.
options.C: An experiment for which the outcome cannot be predicted with certainty before it is performed.
options.D: An experiment that always yields the same result.

mcqs.answer: An experiment for which the outcome cannot be predicted with certainty before it is performed.
mcqs.explanation: A random experiment is one whose result cannot be predicted with certainty before it is carried out; only the set of possible outcomes is known. Option C captures this definition, while the other options describe deterministic or impossible situations.

mcqs.question: In the context of probability, an "outcome" is best described as:

options.A: A set of all possible results of an experiment.
options.B: A single possible result of a random experiment.
options.D: The probability of an event occurring.

mcqs.answer: A single possible result of a random experiment.
mcqs.explanation: An outcome refers to one specific result that may occur when a random experiment is performed. Option B states this precisely; the other options describe sample spaces, collections of experiments, or probabilities, which are different concepts.

mcqs.question: The sample space of a random experiment is:

options.A: The set of all possible outcomes of that experiment.
options.B: A single outcome that occurs most frequently.
options.C: The set of events that are impossible.

mcqs.answer: The set of all possible outcomes of that experiment.
mcqs.explanation: The sample space (denoted S) contains every outcome that can possibly occur when the experiment is carried out. Options B, C, and D describe unrelated ideas such as mode, impossible events, or probability distributions.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly defines an event in probability?

options.A: A single outcome of a random experiment.
options.B: A subset of the sample space consisting of one or more outcomes.
options.C: The total number of possible outcomes.
options.D: The probability assigned to each outcome.

mcqs.answer: A subset of the sample space consisting of one or more outcomes.
mcqs.explanation: An event is any collection (subset) of outcomes from the sample space. It may contain one outcome (elementary) or many (compound). Option B captures this; the other options describe an outcome, the size of the sample space, or probabilities, which are not definitions of an event.

mcqs.question: In tossing a fair coin twice, which of the following correctly identifies an elementary event and a compound event?

options.A: Getting heads on the first toss (elementary) and getting at least one head in two tosses (compound).
options.B: Getting heads on the first toss (compound) and getting at least one head (elementary).
options.C: Getting two tails (elementary) and getting a head on the first toss (compound).
options.D: Getting two heads (elementary) and getting exactly one head (compound).

mcqs.answer: Getting two heads (elementary) and getting exactly one head (compound).
mcqs.explanation: An elementary event corresponds to a single specific outcome, such as the ordered pair (H,H) i.e., two heads. "Exactly one head" includes two possible outcomes (H,T) and (T,H), making it a compound event. Option D states this correctly; the other options misclassify the events.

mcqs.question: A student draws a card from a well‑shuffled standard deck of 52 cards and records its suit. Which description best characterizes this situation?

options.A: A deterministic experiment because the suit can be known in advance.
options.B: A random experiment because the outcome (the suit) cannot be predicted with certainty before drawing.
options.C: A repeated experiment that always yields the same result.
options.D: An experiment with no sample space.

mcqs.answer: A random experiment because the outcome (the suit) cannot be predicted with certainty before drawing.
mcqs.explanation: Drawing a card from a shuffled deck is random: before the draw, any of the four suits could appear, and we cannot know which one will be obtained. Hence it fits the definition of a random experiment. Options A, C, and D are incorrect because the outcome is not predetermined, not always the same, and a clear sample space (the four suits) exists.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about an outcome is FALSE?

options.A: An outcome is one possible result of a random experiment.
options.B: All outcomes together form the sample space.
options.C: An outcome can be a set of multiple results.
options.D: Each outcome is mutually exclusive with other outcomes.

mcqs.answer: An outcome can be a set of multiple results.
mcqs.explanation: An outcome is a single result, not a set. Options A, B, and D correctly describe outcomes: each is a possible result, the collection of all outcomes makes the sample space, and distinct outcomes cannot occur simultaneously. Option C misrepresents the definition, making it the false statement.

mcqs.question: If a die is rolled, which of the following correctly represents the sample space and why?

options.A: {1,2,3,4,5,6} because these are all possible results of a single die roll.
options.B: {2,4,6} because only even numbers can appear.
options.C: {1,2,3,4,5,6,7} because the die may show any number up to 7.
options.D: ∅ because no outcome is possible before rolling.

mcqs.answer: {1,2,3,4,5,6} because these are all possible results of a single die roll.
mcqs.explanation: When a standard six‑sided die is rolled, the only possible results are the integers 1 through 6, forming the sample space {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Options B and C list incorrect sets, and D incorrectly claims no outcomes exist before the experiment. Hence option A is correct.
